implementation_notes: The persistence provider owns the token: annotate exactly one field or property with @Version (int, Integer, long, Long, short, Short or java.sql.Timestamp) and otherwise work with the entity normally - the provider reads the version with the entity, adds the version predicate to the UPDATE it generates and throws jakarta.persistence.OptimisticLockException when zero rows match, marking the transaction for rollback; Jakarta Persistence 3.0 requires Java 8 or later. The classic structure is therefore absorbed by the ORM and only conflict resolution is left to the application: catch the exception in a fresh transaction, re-read, merge and retry. Keep a hand-written form when there is no provider on the classpath or the write is set-based - JDBC PreparedStatement.executeUpdate() with the version in the WHERE clause and the returned count as the test, or AtomicLong.compareAndSet for in-process state.
pitfalls: The application must not modify the @Version attribute; a user-assigned value can make providers skip or corrupt the check.
A versioned entity has exactly one version attribute and it must live in the primary table, so joined-inheritance mappings need the token on the root entity.
After OptimisticLockException the transaction is marked for rollback: catching it inside the same transaction and continuing leaves the persistence context unusable - resolve in a fresh transaction.
Bulk JPQL/CriteriaUpdate statements bypass version checks and never increment the token.

variants.name: Hand-written JDBC conditional write with rowcount test
variants.implementation_notes: Without a persistence provider the check is application code: prepare the UPDATE (or DELETE) with AND version = ? in the WHERE clause, bind the token that was read with the row, and branch on executeUpdate() returning 0; keep it inside the same transaction that performed the read. For a shared in-process record the token becomes java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong and compareAndSet(expected, expected + 1) is the check, with the failed call handing back the current value for a re-read. This variant is more verbose and easier to get wrong than the annotation, but it is the only route when JPA is not on the classpath and the only one that scales to set-based statements where you must consciously decide how the token behaves.
pitfalls: Autocommit turns the read and the conditional write into separate transactions, which re-opens the lost update even though the predicate is correct.
Comparing AtomicLong.compareAndSet against a value captured before another writer's successful exchange is a test on the token only - pair it with re-reading the payload.
